q: The graph traces part of a radioactive decay series on a plot of neutron number against proton number. It starts at neptunium-237 (A) and passes through B, C, D and E to F. What is nuclide F?
h: Read Z and N for point F from the axes. The mass number is A = Z + N, and Z identifies the element.
w: Point F sits at Z = 89 and N = 136, so A = 89 + 136 = 225, and Z = 89 is actinium: 22589Ac. The path shows A → B and C → D → E as α steps (Z and N each drop by 2) and B → C and E → F as β− steps (one neutron becomes a proton). 22588Ra is point E, A = 226 comes from adding Z and the N of E, and 22187Fr would be one more α step.
x: This is point E. The last step raises Z by one, which is a β⁻ decay.
Recheck the mass number. A is Z plus N for point F itself.
That would follow from one more alpha decay after F. Read F’s own coordinates.

q: The natural logarithm of the activity of a radioactive sample (in counts per minute) is plotted against time. What is the half-life of the isotope?
h: Radioactive decay is first order, so ln(activity) vs time is a straight line whose slope is −k. Then t<sub>1/2</sub> = 0.693/k.
w: Slope = (6.90 − 9.21)/(100 − 0) min = −0.0231 min−1, so k = 0.0231 min−1 and t1/2 = 0.693/0.0231 = 30 min. 43 min is 1/k (it leaves out ln 2), 15 min is half of the half-life, and 60 min is the time for the activity to fall to one quarter.
x: This is 1/k. The half-life is ln 2 divided by k.
At 15 min ln(activity) has dropped by only about 0.35, not by ln 2 (0.693).
By this time ln(activity) has dropped by about 1.39, which is two half-lives.

q:
The graph shows the number of undecayed atoms in two radioactive samples, X and Y, that each start with 1000 atoms. Which statements are true?
I. X has the shorter half-life.
II. At t = 0, sample X has the greater activity.
III. After 6 h, sample Y has four times as many undecayed atoms as sample X.
h: Read each half-life where the curve crosses 500 atoms. Activity = kN, and k is larger for the shorter half-life.
w: I is true: X reaches 500 atoms at 2 h, Y at 6 h. II is true: both start with 1000 atoms, and activity = kN with k = 0.693/t1/2, so X (larger k) decays three times as fast at t = 0. III is true: after 6 h, X has gone through 3 half-lives (125 atoms) and Y through 1 (500 atoms), a ratio of 4. Answer: I, II and III.
x: Statements II and III are also true. Equal numbers of atoms decay faster when the half-life is shorter, and read both curves at 6 h.
Statement III is also true. Read both curves at 6 h and compare.
Statement II is also true. With the same number of atoms, the shorter half-life means more decays per second.

q: The shaded area is the band of stability on a plot of neutrons versus protons; the gray line is N = Z. Nuclide R (calcium-54: Z = 20, N = 34) is marked. Which equation shows its most likely mode of decay?
c: 5420Ca → 5421Sc + 0−1e
5420Ca → 5419K + 0+1e
5420Ca → 5018Ar + 42He
5420Ca + 0−1e → 5419K
h: R lies above the band, so its neutron-to-proton ratio is too high. Which process turns a neutron into a proton?
w: R sits above the band (too many neutrons for 20 protons). β− emission converts a neutron into a proton, lowering N by 1 and raising Z by 1, which moves R toward the band: 5420Ca → 5421Sc + 0−1e. Positron emission and electron capture both turn a proton into a neutron, which suits nuclides below the band, and α emission is typical of heavy nuclides with Z > 83.
x: Positron emission turns a proton into a neutron, which would raise the already high neutron to proton ratio.
Alpha decay is typical of very heavy nuclides, beyond about Z = 83. Calcium is far lighter.
Electron capture turns a proton into a neutron, which suits nuclides below the band, not above it.

q: The boxes show the particles of a nucleus before and after it decays (red = proton, gray = neutron, small blue = electron). What type of decay is shown?
h: Count protons and neutrons in each box, and note whether a particle appears or disappears.
w: Before: 5 protons and 7 neutrons (boron-12). After: 6 protons, 6 neutrons and an emitted electron. A neutron turned into a proton and an electron, the mass number stayed at 12, and Z rose by 1 (boron-12 → carbon-12): β− emission. Positron emission and electron capture both lower Z, and α emission removes 2 protons and 2 neutrons.
x: Positron emission turns a proton into a neutron. Here the number of protons went up.
In electron capture an electron is absorbed and Z drops. Here an electron appears and Z rises.
Alpha emission removes two protons and two neutrons together. The nucleon total here is still 12.

q: The boxes show a sample of a radioactive isotope at t = 0 and 10.0 minutes later (purple = radioactive parent atom, yellow = stable daughter atom). What is the half-life of the parent isotope?
h: Find the fraction of parent atoms left, then how many halvings produce that fraction.
w: Parent atoms fall from 16 to 4, one quarter of the original. 16 → 8 → 4 is two half-lives, so 2 t1/2 = 10.0 min and t1/2 = 5.0 min. 10.0 min would leave 8 parent atoms, and 6.7 min assumes the atoms decay at a constant (linear) rate instead of halving.
x: After one half-life 8 parent atoms would remain. Only 4 are left.
After 10.0 min this would be four half-lives, leaving only 1 parent atom.
Radioactive decay halves the amount each half-life rather than removing the same number per minute.

q: A heavy element was first made by firing iron-58 nuclei at a bismuth-209 target, as shown. One neutron is released. What is the product nucleus?

f.text: 20983Bi + 5826Fe → ? + 10n

h: Mass numbers (top) and atomic numbers (bottom) must each add up to the same total on both sides.
w: Mass: 209 + 58 = 267 = A + 1, so A = 266. Atomic number: 83 + 26 = 109 = Z + 0, so Z = 109, meitnerium: 266109Mt. A = 267 forgets the neutron; Z = 110 or 108 would leave the atomic numbers unbalanced.
x: This forgets the neutron that leaves, which carries one unit of mass number.
Recheck the atomic numbers: 83 plus 26 does not give 110.
Recheck the atomic numbers: a neutron has Z = 0, so no protons are lost.

q: A sample of a medical radioisotope gives the activities in the first table. Which isotope in the second table is it most likely to be?
h: Find the time it takes the activity to drop to half of its starting value.
w: The activity falls from 800 to 400 counts/min in 6.0 h, and to 200 (one quarter) at 12.0 h, so t1/2 = 6.0 h: technetium-99m. 12 h is two half-lives, not one, so iodine-123 does not fit; fluorine-18 would have dropped to almost nothing by 12 h, and sodium-24 would still be above 400 at 12 h.
x: At 12 h the activity is one quarter of the start, which is two half-lives, not one.
With a 1.83 h half-life the activity would fall to about 26 counts/min in 9 h.
With a 15 h half-life the activity would still be above 400 counts/min after 12 h.

q: The box represents the uranium and lead atoms in a tiny crystal of zircon. Assume the crystal contained no lead when it formed, so all of the lead-206 came from uranium-238 decay (t<sub>1/2</sub> = 4.47×10<sup>9</sup> yr). How old is the crystal?
h: Each Pb-206 atom was once a U-238 atom. Find the original number of U atoms, the fraction remaining, and use ln(N<sub>0</sub>/N) = kt.
w: The box has 16 U and 4 Pb atoms, so the crystal began with 20 U atoms and 16/20 = 0.800 remain. k = 0.693/(4.47×109 yr) = 1.55×10−10 yr−1; t = ln(20/16)/k = 0.223/1.55×10−10 = 1.44×109 yr (1.439e+9). 1.86×109 yr takes 75% (12 of 16) as the fraction left, 1.12×109 yr treats decay as linear, and 8.94×109 yr is two half-lives.
x: The 16 uranium atoms are what remain of 20 original atoms, so the fraction left is 16 out of 20.
Radioactive decay is exponential, so the time is not simply proportional to the fraction decayed.
Two half-lives would leave only a quarter of the uranium. Most of the uranium is still present.

q:
Which of these nuclear equations represent nuclear fission?
I. 21H + 31H → 42He + 10n
II. 23994Pu + 10n → 13454Xe + 10340Zr + 3 10n
III. 24195Am → 23793Np + 42He
h: Fission splits a heavy nucleus into two medium-sized nuclei, usually after it absorbs a neutron. Emitting a small particle is ordinary radioactive decay.
w: I is not fission: two very light nuclei join, which is fusion. II is fission: plutonium-239 absorbs a neutron and splits into two mid-sized nuclei (Xe and Zr) plus 3 neutrons (mass 240 = 134 + 103 + 3; charge 94 = 54 + 40). III is not fission: americium-241 emits a small α particle, which is α decay. Answer: II only.
x: Equation I joins two light nuclei, which is fusion, the opposite of fission.
Equation III is alpha decay. A helium nucleus leaves, but the nucleus is not split into two mid-sized pieces.
Equations I and III are fusion and alpha decay. Only one equation splits a heavy nucleus.

q: Smoke detectors contain americium-241, which decays by emitting alpha particles. Which equation correctly shows this decay?
c: 24195Am → 23793Np + 42He
24195Am → 23791Pa + 42He
24195Am → 24196Cm + 0−1e
24195Am + 42He → 24597Bk
h: An alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus, with mass number 4 and atomic number 2. It leaves the nucleus.
w: Emitting 42He lowers the mass number by 4 (241 → 237) and the atomic number by 2 (95 → 93, neptunium): 24195Am → 23793Np + 42He. Subtracting 4 from Z gives Pa and unbalances the charges, the Cm equation is β− decay, and the Bk equation absorbs an α particle instead of emitting one.
x: The alpha particle carries 2 protons, not 4. Check that the atomic numbers balance.
This equation emits an electron, which is beta decay, not alpha decay.
Here the alpha particle is absorbed. In alpha decay it is emitted.

q: The boxes show the particles of an oxygen-15 nucleus before and after it decays (red = proton, gray = neutron, small yellow = the particle released). Which nuclear equation matches the drawing?
c: 158O → 157N + 0+1e
158O → 159F + 0−1e
158O + 0−1e → 157N
158O → 147N + 11H
h: Count protons and neutrons before and after. The released particle is tiny and positively charged.
w: Before: 8 p, 7 n. After: 7 p, 8 n, plus a small positive particle. A proton became a neutron and a positron left the nucleus: 158O → 157N + 0+1e. β− emission would raise Z to 9, electron capture absorbs a particle instead of releasing one, and proton emission would leave 7 p and 7 n.
x: Beta emission turns a neutron into a proton, so Z would rise. In the drawing Z falls from 8 to 7.
Electron capture absorbs an electron and releases nothing charged. The drawing shows a particle released.
Losing a proton would leave 7 protons and 7 neutrons. The drawing shows 8 neutrons after the decay.

q: The table lists three samples of different radioisotopes. Rank them in order of INCREASING activity (decays per second).
h: Activity = kN, and k = 0.693/t<sub>1/2</sub>. Compare N/t<sub>1/2</sub> for each sample.
w: Activity is proportional to N/t1/2: I, 1.0/10 = 0.10; II, 4.0/20 = 0.20; III, 0.50/2.0 = 0.25 (mol per day). So I < II < III. Ranking by half-life alone gives II < I < III, ranking by amount alone gives III < I < II, and the last order treats a longer half-life as more active.
x: This ranks by half-life only. Sample II has four times as many atoms as sample I.
This ranks by amount only. A short half-life makes each atom far more likely to decay.
A longer half-life means slower decay, so this order runs the wrong way.

q: Cobalt-60 for cancer therapy is made by placing cobalt-59 in a nuclear reactor, as shown. What is the missing product?

f.text: 5927Co + 10n → 6027Co + ?

h: Compare the mass numbers and atomic numbers on the two sides. What is left over for the missing product?
w: Mass: 59 + 1 = 60 + A, so A = 0. Atomic number: 27 + 0 = 27 + Z, so Z = 0. A particle with no mass number and no charge is a gamma ray: 00γ. An electron has Z = −1, a proton has A = 1 and Z = 1, and a neutron has A = 1, so none of them balances.
x: An electron carries a −1 charge, which would leave the atomic numbers unbalanced.
A proton has mass number 1 and atomic number 1. Both sides already balance without it.
A neutron has mass number 1, which would leave the mass numbers unbalanced.
